pathway.title: JavaScript Programming
pathway.description: Learn to plan, write, test, and explain small JavaScript programs using clear steps, data, functions, and modules.

course.title: JavaScript Programming — Beginner
course.short_description: A beginner course in JavaScript fundamentals, control flow, functions, arrays, objects, validation, and modules.
course.prerequisites: No programming experience is required. Learners should be able to read simple instructions and use an approved computer or coding environment.
learning_outcomes: Translate a familiar task into inputs, processing steps, and expected outputs.
Write and run JavaScript scripts with variables, operators, strings, and Boolean conditions.
Use branches, loops, and functions to express reusable behavior.
Represent small collections and records with arrays and objects.
Validate input, handle expected errors, and test normal and edge cases.
Organize code with ES modules and explain the limits of local in-memory examples.
course.dependencies: Node.js 20+ built-ins only; no third-party packages required.

modules.title: Start programming with JavaScript
modules.description: Plan algorithms, run JavaScript with Node.js, and name values clearly.

topics.title: Think in steps: algorithms and programs
topics.description: Describe a problem as inputs, ordered steps, and outputs before writing JavaScript.

lesson.title: Think in steps: algorithms and programs
objectives: Explain how an algorithm differs from a program.
Break a familiar task into ordered, unambiguous steps.
Identify inputs, processing, and outputs in a small coding problem.

blocks.title: Core idea
blocks.body: A computer follows instructions; it does not guess what someone meant. An algorithm is a finite, ordered plan for solving a problem, while a program expresses instructions in a language a computer can run. Before coding, name the inputs, the processing, and the output. For a simple reading-list helper, the inputs might be two practice prices, the process could add them, and the output is the total. Clear steps expose missing information: “calculate the result” is vague until we know what to calculate and how to present it. A programmer can write steps in plain language, pseudocode, or a flow diagram before translating them into JavaScript. This habit helps beginners focus on reasoning rather than punctuation. It also gives a simple way to check a program: compare what it actually does with the plan and the expected result.

topics.title: Run JavaScript and display output
topics.description: Use Node.js to run a small script and distinguish source code from program output.

lesson.title: Run JavaScript and display output
objectives: Describe the roles of a JavaScript file and the Node.js runtime.
Use `console.log()` to display text and values.
Recognize comments and a basic syntax error.

blocks.title: Core idea
blocks.body: JavaScript is a programming language. Node.js is a runtime that can execute JavaScript outside a web browser, which makes it useful for small scripts and beginner exercises. Save code in a text file ending in `.mjs` and run it with a recent Node.js version, or use an approved coding environment that supports JavaScript. The `console.log()` function displays values in the terminal. Text needs matching quotation marks, while a calculation such as `2 + 3` is evaluated before its result is displayed. A comment beginning with `//` helps a human reader and is not executed as an instruction. Syntax is the language's spelling and structure. A missing quote, bracket, or parenthesis may stop the file before it runs. Read the first error and the line it identifies, then inspect nearby punctuation. Source code and output are related, but output is the result of running the source, not another spelling of the code.

topics.title: Name values with const and let
topics.description: Store data in descriptive variables and recognize common JavaScript primitive types.

lesson.title: Name values with const and let
objectives: Choose descriptive names for variables.
Use `const` for bindings that are not reassigned and `let` when reassignment is needed.
Recognize string, number, and Boolean values.

blocks.title: Core idea
blocks.body: A variable name gives a value a useful label. JavaScript uses `const` for a binding that will not be reassigned and `let` when the binding needs a new value later. Prefer `const` when possible because it makes changes easier to spot. A `const` object may still have its properties changed; the binding itself cannot point to a different object. Strings hold text in quotes, numbers represent whole or decimal values, and Booleans are `true` or `false`. JavaScript has one ordinary `number` type for both whole and decimal numeric values. Names such as `bookTitle` or `pageCount` communicate meaning better than `x`. Use consistent casing, usually camelCase for variables and function names. Do not use reserved words as names. Readability matters more than clever abbreviations, especially when a program will be revisited or explained to another person.

topics.title: Calculate with numbers and convert text carefully
topics.description: Use arithmetic operators, explicit conversions, and checks for invalid numeric input.

lesson.title: Calculate with numbers and convert text carefully
objectives: Use arithmetic operators for totals and averages.
Convert numeric text with `Number()` before arithmetic.
Check for invalid values with `Number.isNaN()` or `Number.isFinite()`.

blocks.title: Core idea
blocks.body: JavaScript arithmetic uses `+`, `-`, `*`, and `/`; parentheses make an intended order easier to read. The `+` operator can add numbers or join strings, so a value's type matters. If a program receives digits as text, convert them deliberately with `Number(text)` before calculating. Conversion is not proof that the result is valid: `Number("twelve")` produces `NaN`, a special number value meaning “not a number.” Use `Number.isNaN()` or `Number.isFinite()` to check a conversion before using it. Avoid relying on implicit conversion, which can produce surprising results when a string and number are mixed. Store intermediate values with descriptive names, and state units when they matter to a reader. The example uses fictional counts, not payments or personal records. Testing both valid and invalid text is important because real input is not always formatted as expected.

topics.title: Build and clean text with template literals
topics.description: Combine text values, normalize whitespace, and format readable messages.

lesson.title: Build and clean text with template literals
objectives: Create and inspect string values.
Use `trim()` and `toLowerCase()` for text preparation.
Insert values into a template literal with `${...}`.

blocks.title: Core idea
blocks.body: A string stores text. JavaScript allows single quotes, double quotes, or backticks to create a string, but matching delimiters are needed. A template literal uses backticks and can insert a value with `${expression}`. This makes a message easier to read than combining many strings with plus signs. Methods such as `trim()` and `toLowerCase()` return a new string; they do not mutate the original text. Trimming can remove accidental spaces at the start and end, and lowercasing can help with case-insensitive comparison. It does not remove spaces between words or provide full language-aware name matching. Keep an original display form when you need to show the exact capitalization a person entered, and use a normalized copy for comparison. Practice with fictional book titles only; do not ask learners to enter private identifiers. Clear labels and careful normalization make small programs friendlier and easier to test.

topics.title: Compare values and combine Boolean conditions
topics.description: Use strict equality and logical operators to express reliable conditions.

lesson.title: Compare values and combine Boolean conditions
objectives: Compare values using strict equality and relational operators.
Explain the Boolean result of a comparison.
Combine simple conditions with `&&`, `||`, and `!`.

blocks.title: Core idea
blocks.body: A comparison asks a question and produces a Boolean value: `true` or `false`. Use `===` for strict equality, which compares both value and type, and `!==` for strict inequality. Relational operators such as `<`, `<=`, `>`, and `>=` compare values such as numbers. Avoid the loose equality operator `==` as a beginner because it may convert types before comparing them. Logical `&&` means both conditions must be true, `||` means at least one must be true, and `!` reverses a Boolean. Parentheses can make a longer condition easier to understand. Test each part separately before combining conditions. A condition should reflect a clear rule, such as whether a fictional item has a positive count and a title that is not empty. Explicit comparisons make a program easier to reason about and reduce accidental truthiness behavior.

topics.title: Make choices with if, else if, and else
topics.description: Create readable branches and deliberately test boundary values.

lesson.title: Make choices with if, else if, and else
objectives: Write a condition using `if` and `else`.
Add an `else if` branch when multiple cases are needed.
Test values around a decision boundary.

blocks.title: Core idea
blocks.body: A conditional lets a program choose which instructions to run. An `if` branch runs when its condition is true; `else if` checks another condition when earlier ones were false; `else` handles the remaining case. Curly braces mark each block, and indentation makes the structure readable even though JavaScript does not require indentation for syntax. Order matters: a broad condition placed first can prevent a more specific branch from running. For a score classification, test just below, exactly at, and just above the threshold. These boundary cases reveal mistakes such as using `>` when the requirement includes equality. Conditions should describe the rule in plain language before translating it into operators. Keep each branch focused, and avoid deeply nested decisions until a simpler structure is clear. The example uses a fictional practice score and does not represent any real learner's assessment result.

topics.title: Repeat work with for and while loops
topics.description: Choose a loop that fits the repetition and make its stopping rule clear.

lesson.title: Repeat work with for and while loops
objectives: Use a `for` loop to repeat a known number of times.
Use `for...of` to visit values in an array.
Explain how a `while` loop reaches its stopping condition.

blocks.title: Core idea
blocks.body: A loop repeats a block of instructions. A `for` loop is useful when the number of repetitions is known, and `for...of` can visit each value in an array. A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition remains true. If the code never changes a value that affects the condition, the loop may run forever. Before running a loop, predict how many times it should execute and what changes between iterations. Use clear variable names such as `index` or `item`. The loop body belongs inside braces; consistent indentation helps readers see it. Avoid changing an array while looping over it until you understand how that affects iteration. A clear stopping rule is part of the algorithm, not an afterthought. Try small sequences first and compare the output with a written prediction to catch off-by-one mistakes.

topics.title: Write reusable functions and return values
topics.description: Define functions with parameters, return results, and separate calculation from display.

lesson.title: Write reusable functions and return values
objectives: Declare a function with parameters.
Return a value for the caller to use.
Distinguish `return` from `console.log()`.

blocks.title: Core idea
blocks.body: A function is a named set of instructions that can be called when needed. A parameter is a name in the function definition that receives a value; an argument is the actual value supplied by a caller. A function can return a result with `return`, allowing another part of the program to store it, display it, or use it in another calculation. `console.log()` displays a value but does not substitute for returning it. Keep each function focused on one clear task, and choose a name that describes the action. The function body goes inside braces. It runs when called, not merely when the function is declared. Calling the same function with different arguments demonstrates reuse. Small functions are easier to test because they have a clear input and output. Avoid hidden side effects while learning; a predictable return value makes the behavior easier to understand.

topics.title: Store ordered collections in arrays
topics.description: Create arrays, use zero-based indexes, add values, and iterate safely.

lesson.title: Store ordered collections in arrays
objectives: Create an array and read an item by index.
Add a value with `push()` and inspect the array length.
Use a loop to process array values.

blocks.title: Core idea
blocks.body: An array stores an ordered collection of values. Square brackets create an array, and commas separate its items. JavaScript uses zero-based indexing: index 0 refers to the first item and index 1 to the second. The `length` property reports how many values are present, and `push(value)` adds a value to the end. Accessing a position that does not exist returns `undefined`, so check the array or use a loop when the size may vary. A `for...of` loop visits the values in order without requiring a manual index. Arrays can contain values of different types, but using a consistent shape makes beginner programs easier to understand. This example stores fictional titles in memory. The values disappear when the script ends because persistent storage is not part of this lesson. Predict the length and indexes before running the code to catch off-by-one errors.

topics.title: Group related values in objects
topics.description: Represent one record with named properties and update a property deliberately.

lesson.title: Group related values in objects
objectives: Create an object with descriptive properties.
Read and update a property with dot notation.
Use a list of similar objects for simple in-memory records.

blocks.title: Core idea
blocks.body: An object groups related information under named properties. Curly braces contain property names and values, such as `title: "Mti"`. Read a value with dot notation like `book.title`, or bracket notation when the property name is dynamic. Assigning to an existing property updates its value. Objects make it easier to understand a record because each value has a label instead of relying on a fixed position. A list of similar objects can represent multiple records, and a loop can examine each one. Keep property names consistent across records; a typo can produce `undefined` instead of the expected value. This lesson uses fictional book details only. An in-memory object is not a database, does not enforce privacy or access controls, and disappears when the script ends. Choose clear property names and make sure the values have the expected type before using them.

topics.title: Handle errors and organize code into modules
topics.description: Validate values, use try/catch for expected failures, and recognize JavaScript modules.

lesson.title: Handle errors and organize code into modules
objectives: Throw and catch a clear error for invalid input.
Explain how ES modules share code with `export` and `import`.
Test normal and invalid cases with explicit expectations.

blocks.title: Core idea
blocks.body: A runtime error occurs while a program is executing, while a syntax error prevents it from being parsed. Validate values at the boundary where they enter a function, and give a clear reason when a value is invalid. `try` and `catch` can handle an expected failure and let a program show a useful message instead of stopping unexpectedly. Do not catch every possible error silently; an unknown problem should remain visible so it can be investigated. As a program grows, ES modules let one file export a function or value and another file import it. A `.mjs` file is treated as an ES module by Node.js. Keep each module focused and use explicit names. Small tests should cover a normal case and an invalid case. Organizing code does not automatically make it correct; modules still need clear responsibilities and tests. This example uses a built-in Node module so it can run without installing packages.

practical_project.title: Fictional Reading Shelf Catalog
practical_project.purpose: Build a small JavaScript program that manages a short in-memory collection of fictional book titles. Use functions, arrays, objects, decisions, validation, and tests to make the behavior clear. The result is a learning exercise, not a production library system or persistent database.
privacy_and_limits: Use invented titles and practice values only; do not enter real learner names, contact details, school records, or borrowing histories.
Keep the program local and in memory. Do not connect it to a real library, school database, account, payment service, or external API.
A successful local exercise does not prove security, persistence, or production readiness; document those limits explicitly.
requirements: Create an array that stores book objects with a trimmed title and an availability Boolean.
Write a function that accepts a title, rejects empty input, and prevents duplicate titles without case sensitivity.
Write a search function that returns matching titles without changing their original display capitalization.
Write a function to update availability and report whether a matching title was found.
Use `const` for stable bindings and `let` only when reassignment is needed; use clear camelCase names.
Validate values and handle expected errors with a clear message rather than silently hiding failures.
Add tests for normal, duplicate, empty, case-variation, and missing-title cases.
Provide a short README with run instructions for Node.js 20+, examples, and privacy/scope limits.
suggested_steps: Write the input, processing, and output requirements in plain language; choose invented test titles.
Create the array of objects and sketch the properties before writing functions.
Implement one focused function at a time, then test its returned values and edge cases.
Connect the functions in a short script that prints a clear demonstration.
Split reusable functions into ES modules if useful, and import them from the demonstration script.
Review readability, tests, expected errors, and the limits of in-memory storage before presenting the project.
success_checks: The program adds a cleaned title once and rejects empty or duplicate titles.
Search compares titles without case sensitivity but preserves display capitalization.
Availability updates return a truthful success or not-found result.
Tests cover normal and edge cases, including case variation and empty input.
The README explains how to run the local program and does not claim production storage or security.

rubric.look_for: Clear functions, descriptive camelCase names, and readable control flow.
Consistent book object shape and correct collection handling.
Trimmed input, empty-title rejection, and case-insensitive duplicate protection.
Search preserves display text and updates only a matching record.
Normal and edge-case checks with clear, non-silent expected-error handling.
Reproducible Node.js instructions and explicit privacy, memory, and production limitations.
